content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces a novel loss term, which encourages high topological similarity, in the context of emergent communication. The paper hypothesizes that increasing the topological similarity of utterances from the two agents will increase the generalization ability of the agents to unseen inputs.

The paper presents evidence that mmoderate amounts of compositional pressure do improve the generalization ability, but large amounts of compositional pressure negatively affect the generalization ability.

The paper goes on to show evidence that the correlation between topological similarity of utterances and the generalization ability is complex and not always clear-cut.
content.main_review:
## Good points

- investigates the use of topological similarity as a loss term, in the context of emergent communication, which loss term might be novel
- presents additional data points showing that the link between topological similarity and generalization is tenuous

## Bad points

- adding topological similarity as a loss term seems to me to fly in the face of the goals of emergent communication, which is to allow the agents to freely generate their own language, and then to evaluate the resulting language? This is not to say that the approach espoused is not useful, but I feel the motivation provided seems unclear to me?
- no code provided
- experiments do not appear to me to eliminate the possibility that the role of the compositional pressure is purely as a regularizer. e.g. can the results be reproduced by using other regularizers such as dropout, L1 weight reg, or L2 weight reg?

## Notes

I wrote the following notes whilst reading through the paper

### Abstract

interesting idea to incorporate metric of compositionality into learning
- doesnt this go against the idea of letting languages emerge naturally, and then evaluating them?
- what is the intention of doing this?
- as far as generatlization vs compositoinality, there is existing work that shows this, eg baroni, kharitonov, andreas

### 1. Introduction

obverter reference seems incorrect to me: I believe you are thinking of Choi et al 2018, not Lazararidou et al 2016?

The introduction seems to me well-written, and fairly complete, on the whole.

However, given the clear knowledge of prior work expressed in the introduction, I'm unclear why the observation that there is no simple correlation between generalization and compositionality is novel? There are multiple works (eg Chaabouni et al 2020, which you cited), which show this already?

Contributions 2 and 3 appear to be highly related to contribution 4.

Using a compositional metric to guide learning seems to me to be novel, but also seems to me to be somewhat against the spirit of emergent communication? i.e. the goal of emergent communication appears to me to be to let languages emerge, and then see what kinds of languages emerge; rather than to add our opinion of ideal languages into the loss function? Nevertheless, it does appear to me to be novel to add the compositional metric into the loss function. Measuring the same metric as our output seems somewhat circular, but measuring generalization ability seems a plausibly reasonable thing to do, to me.

### 2. Language emergence game

I thought the paragraphs were going in the direction of using non-symbolic input, so I was a bit disappointed to find their arguing in favor of symbolic inputs.

#### 2.1 setup

Nice that you are using the recommended notation for sets for ICLR :)

#### 2.2 agents

I don't understand what you are pairing. You suddnely talk about it, out of nowhere. From my understanding, for each example, we take a single object, x, which is sampled from N_A attributes, each with N_V possible values. We feed this through our network, which predicts what was the original x. There is no negative sampling involved. I'm not sure I understand what the pairs relate to. Please could you explain the pairing motivation more clearly?

## 3. Pressure for compositionality

### 3.1 Metrics for compositionality

Ok, this bit explains taht the pairwise is for topological similarity. However, I feel the ordering of the explanation wrt the text in 2.2 makes the text in 2.2 challenging to understand. I feel it might be good to rethink the ordering of these texts a little?

Interesting observation that Pearson correlation is differentiable.

## 4. Experiments

Figure 1: I feel that 1e-6 should be in between 0.0 and 0.1 in the legend?

Why are the random seeds 1,3,5,7,11,13? why not just choose 1,2,3,4,5,6?

I'm not sure what it means for an exampoe to be 'up to five times the size of the input space'?

I believe 'thrive' might be intended to be 'strive'?

Figure 1: you are dnoeted message space size as eg (10,4), but I believe per your notation, defined in 2.1, this hsould be written M(10, 4)? This would alo reduce my confusion, since I initially assumed taht (10,4) was input space size, not message space size.

$C_t$ is not defined in the text. It's implicitly defined in algorithm 1. It's obviously the coefficient in front of the topological similarity regularization term, however I think it would be good to state this explicitly in the text?

I find figure 1 hard to read: I think we care about seeing the effect of $C_t$? Therefore, strong preference for the x axis to be $C_t$. and for the runs, rather than showing training curves, why not use early stopping somehow (or just train always for 100 epochs, as you state in the text), and report the value either at early stopping, or at 100 epochs? Then you can draw a single curve of test accuracy vs C_t. And you can put all six curves, for each different message space, on the same set of axes. I believe this would be much more intuitive for me to understand/read.

### 4.1 Generalization

Why do you test with both recurrent and linear architecture for hte listener? Why not just choose one, to keep things simple?

"It is evident from the plots that there is no clear winner for Ct, which is suitable for all the scenarios." => not obvious at all to me tbh. Not without looking really carefully. Please consider redoing the plots ,as alluded to above, so that it is in fact really obvious :)

The graphs are all for linear listener. In reality, in emergent communication literature, almost all listeners I've ever seen are some kind of RNN. I think it might be more meaningful then to just use an RNN listener, and move linear listener results into the appendix?

### 4.2 Compositionality

You compare your compositional loss term to other regularization techniques. How do you know that the term is not functioning simply as a regularization term? For example, what happens if you flip the compositionality term, so that it encourages low compositionality. This would also act as a regularizer, by increasing entropy. Does this also increase test accuracy too.

"Excessive compositional pressure" implies that the compositional pressure is bad, but if I understand correctly, in this context the high compositional pressure is actually good, for test accuracy? So, perhaps use "High compositional pressure" instead of "Excessive compositional pressure"?

Don't your results at M(50,2) align with a hypothesis that the compositionality loss could be acting uniquely as a regularizer, rather than by improving something concrete that correlates with generalization?

"However there is more than enough evidence to accept advantage of the compositional pressure on generalization" => I feel this is overly strong. There is some small amount of evidence, but nuanced by at least 1. high compositional pressure reduces test accuracy, and 2. the hypothesis that it is acting purely as any other regularizer. e.g. what happens if you use other regularizers such as L1 weight norm, L2 weight norm, or dropout? Can you reproduce similar graphs as for using compositional pressure?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper investigates the use of topological similarity as a loss function to improve the generalization ability of agents, in the context of emergent communication. I feel that this approach is sort of the opposite direction of other emergent communication research, which allows the agents to freely emerge their own language, and then evaluates the resulting language. Thus, I feel it is important to motivate clearly what the goal of the additional loss function is.

The paper does give an additional data point showing that the link between compositionality, as measured by topological similarity, and generalization is tenuous. However, there already exist multiple works that present such evidence, as alluded to in the Related Work section of this work.

The paper shows that the compositional pressure does improve generalization ability, but only in moderation, and that the amount to be used is an empirical question, which depends on many factors, in a complex way. Thus, is it different from any other regularizer? Could a similar effect be observed by using other regularizers such as dropout, or weight decay?

Overall, I feel that I'd like to see the paper delve in a little deeper somehow. For example, comparing to other regularizers, comparing with applying negative compositional pressure. How do agents with naturally high compositionality compare with those which had high compositionality under conditions of high compositional pressure? How do other metrics of compositionality change? Can we apply compositional pressure using other metrics, such as Resnick's residual entropy?

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer WEY2 (1/2)
content.comment:
First, the authors highly thank the reviewer, for their invaluable comments to improve the paper, and their quick response to our previous comments. We will address reviewers' concerns below.

>adding topological similarity as a loss term seems to me to fly in the face of the goals of emergent communication, which is to allow the agents to freely generate their own language, and then to evaluate the resulting language? This is not to say that the approach espoused is not useful, but I feel the motivation provided seems unclear to me?

In the current draft, we only measure compositionality for the cases where we do not employ any type of compositionality loss on the discrete link, which we denote as the baseline scenario. For this case, we study how generalization and compositionality relate, and find that there is indeed a strong but situational correlation.

In the case, where we use compositionality loss, we demonstrate the addition of compositionality loss, if used in controlled amounts, can improve generalization and transmission speed than the baseline cases. We do not intend to highlight the correlation between test accuracy and topological similarity, for this case, since both are now being optimized simultaneously.
Our loss is not based on a mechanism that is seen in the human language evolution process, but we do not think that adding a loss does violate the existing practices of language emergence research. For example, there are several works which employ different types of metrics, which measure quality of communications in a human perspective, on the emerging communications .

Studies have used various losses on emerging messages like; entropy regularization, loss on message length, loss on symbol usage, and selecting messages most understandable to the sender itself [1,2,3]. And humans, like how they try to use the shortest message, use compositional expressions not atomic messages. Hence, we think that adding a compositionality loss, which does not require any additional examples, is not against the existing research. As we understand, the main expectation of language emergence is to develop languages in a grounded manner without explicit supervising examples. In our environment, this property is not violated or removed, and agents still develop communications out of necessity.

We are motivated to induce compositionality for two reasons; First, we observe natural languages are compositional and humans use natural language to express complex concepts, which hints about possible advantages of compositionality. Secondly, there have been studies, using methods motivated by language evolution, that show the generalizing advantage of compositional languages. In this research, we replace the generational transmission mechanisms with a loss which can be directly optimized, which does not need additional training stages.

1. Katrina Evtimova, Andrew Drozdov, Douwe Kiela, and Kyunghyun Cho. Emergent communication in a multi-modal, multi-step referential game. In 6th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2018.


2. Edward Choi, Angeliki Lazaridou, and Nando De Freitas. Compositional obverter communication learning from raw visual input. In 6th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2018.


3. Angeliki Lazaridou, Karl Moritz Hermann, Karl Tuyls, and Stephen Clark. Emergence of linguistic communication from referential games with symbolic and pixel input. In 6th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2018.

>experiments do not appear to me to eliminate the possibility that the role of the compositional pressure is purely as a regularizer. e.g. can the results be reproduced by using other regularizers such as dropout, L1 weight reg, or L2 weight reg?
We have included additional experiments as requested by the reviewer for the cases of dropout and weight decay.

| M(W,L)   | Dropout = 0.5     | Dropout = 0.7  
|----------|-------------------|-------------------|
| M(10,4)  | 0.478 $\pm$ 0.040 | 0.499 $\pm$ 0.002 | 
| M(10,6)  | 0.455 $\pm$ 0.108 | 0.498 $\pm$ 0.001 | 
| M(100,2) | 0.811 $\pm$ 0.365 | 0.512 $\pm$ 0.012 |
| M(100,4) | 0.879 $\pm$ 0.013 | 0.501 $\pm$ 0.009 |

With the experiments with dropout we did not see any improvements over the baseline case for any configuration. In fact the displayed results are less than the baseline scenario. Increasing the dropout has increased the performance for the first two message spaces but for the last two cases, results have been degraded. For these configurations,  even with a very high compositional pressure ($C_t = 1$), test accuracy is still higher than the results gained with dropout = 0.7.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
> we observe natural languages are compositional and humans use natural language to express complex concepts, which hints about possible advantages of compositionality. Secondly, there have been studies, using methods motivated by language evolution, that show the generalizing advantage of compositional languages.

Right. I'm much more interested in understanding how evolution and such gave rise to compositionality. It appears that in our artificial experiments, it emerges only very weakly, for reasons unclear. I'm personally interested in why it doesn't emerge naturally in our experiments, and what needs to change so that it does. However, directly postulating a pre-existing loss function that encourages compositionality seems problematic to me. One would have to then explain where this loss function came from.

In emergent communication literature in general, one supposes some kind of collaborative task (occasionally non-collaborative, or more ambiguous, but usually at least somewhat collaborative), where agents gain a reward for completing the task.

This all seems biologically plausible to me. We can imagine a pair of creatures hunting together, and needing to collaborate in order to hunt effectively. Those who collaborate more effectively kill the prey with higher probability, and are thus both more likely to survive having food), and to reproduce (staying alive, and perhaps being attractive to potential partners).

However, the loss you are adding has no obvious biological plausibility. By what means are you motivating it?

Ok, so you say, paraphrasing "but entropy regularization". Well, yes, that's a challenging point to refute I agree. However, one can see such a thing as being part of the learning/optimizing process (I'm thinking this through... I might end up agreeing with you, unclear a this point...). And one can see the learning/optimizing process as having evolved over time. It's a very general 'thing' that could have evolved in order to learn more basic things, like walking, flying etc.

So, you could argue "but pressure for compositionality" could have evolved too. Yes, but by what kind of mechanism? Not from learning to fly, nor by learning to walk. One would have to posit an advantage to something else. Communicating perhaps? In that case, I think I'd be interested in seeing an experiment that somehow simulates an environment that causes this loss function for pressure on compositionality to emerge naturally.

So, you could argue, "well babysteps. first we should show that a loss function that encourages compositionality shows a benefit. Later on we can make a new paper that shows that pressure to communicate is sufficient for such a loss function to evolve, naturally." And that would be a fair point too.

So, let me open your paper again a sec....

Well, you aren't arguing this case. In fact, you are arguing that your technique is better than evolution. You are positioning your technique as a competitive technique, better than evolution. So, you are not making the argument that I just wrote in your favor. So, I feel you need to write your own argument then. There are no 'rules' as such in emergent communication domain, no-one has rigorously defined what are the 'goals', which are fairly nebulous I feel (there is perhaps an opportunity for someone to write a work synthesizing the various goals; perhaps I can do that sometime...). Still, I feel there needs to be more motivation than just 'score higher on compositional metrics, by adding compositional metrics into the loss'?

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer WEY2
content.comment:
We highly thank the reviewer for their continuous interest.

There are existing research that emerge their language within a single generation of neural agents, as we do in this draft. In that type of research, the languages they emerge, as we think, are not evolving through multiple generations.  Next, we see that existing natural languages are displaying compositional features which help them generalizing, but we do not investigate how these existing languages have become compositional. It may due to evolutionary processes, which we are not refuting. 

Although, we do not employ or study the mechanisms that made the existing natural languages compositional,  what we observe is that, since existing languages are compositional, human learners learn to use language in a compositional manner and it helps generalizing. This acquired compositionality of a single human learner, as we think, is motivated by learning through compositional examples already existing. But in the language emergence it is best to avoid using supervising examples to make sure that agents are free to ground their words with meanings on their own. 

Hence, we use our compositional loss, that does not require explicit linguistic (or communicative) examples, into the loss function. We do not change the original reconstruction loss, therefore we do not think it affects the primary aspects of language emergence; grounding and capturing functional aspects. t is still a non-example based loss and so the compositional loss. Hence, agents  still have much freedom to emerge their own concepts, and  we are only asking them to make their representations compositional.  And we show through our experiments, that such steering can increase the generalizing power and transmissibility. 

We believe, language emergence research have been motivated like explained above; observing the prevailing characteristics of natural languages. For example, most frequently seen communicating link, between agents in language emergence, is in discrete format. We think, this is because it resembles the discrete nature of existing human languages. We do not refuse  evolutionary mechanisms behind the discrete nature of human languages.  But also not refuse the possibility of directly observing the existing natural languages and  obtaining inspiration from its characteristics.  If incorporating them do not restrict the agents from inventing or emerging their own concepts.

>score higher on compositional metrics, by adding compositional metrics into the loss

We are actually not doing this. Of course we measure compositionlaity in a set of experiments, where we do not employ any external pressure, hence it is not circular.

For the second part of experiments, we employ the pressure, which increase the compositionality.  But most importantly we do not present it as the end effect we desire. Our desired end effects are generalization and transmission speed. In the current draft, we show that, the increased compositionality in our communications, improve generalization and transmission speed compared with the baseline. Hence, the advantage offered by incorporating the compositionality loss is, the increase of generalization and transmission speed, not the mere increase of compositionality alone.

We thank the reviewer for their quick responses.

>So that leaves the use of the compositional metric loss to encourage compositionality. But I kind of feel that training on the test loss is a little like training on the test set, in the case of emergent communication?  

We are not intending to do this in our paper.  There are two experiment sets in the draft.

1. Experiments that measure compositionality and generalization, but do not employ any external pressure. In these experiments, we do  not see any problem.

2. Experiments employing compositional pressure: in this case, we are interested in generalization and transmission speed. Hence we do not see any problem in here too. In this draft, we show  experimentally, that our method can improve the transmission speed and the test accuracy. Of course our method increases the compositionality of the emerged languages, but it is not our end result. The end results concern generalization and transmission speed, which we measure and compare with the baseline. We propose our approach as a method that increase these two metrics in conjunction. 

>And as far as your claiming that you show that compositionality makes a language easier to learn, this was observed in many works in the last couple of years, inspired by Kirby's ILM, but also including the same Chaabouni et al paper, at the end of the same introduction:

Actually, we do not  intend to pose as the first to observe this relationship, although our experiments verify this claim. What we do is that we propose a method based on compositional pressure to make languages more transmission friendly as we show in our transmission speed experiments. 

>are you suggesting that we start adding such a loss to our experiments? I don't see myself doing that...

There are multiple functional losses, which we hope, will increase the performance of emergence languages. Instead of using supervising examples, we can create such losses, that mimic desired characteristics and steer language emerging agents to optimize them in a simultaneous manner. We do not think this as a violation of the grounding aspects, since agents are free to invent their own concepts. We hope, by using such functional pressures, the emerging languages could improve considerably.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
This paper is a first in my role as reviewer, in that generally, I feel that the papers I have reviewed before where I've rejected them have simply not gone into enough depth/rigor; and adding depth/rigor would, in my opinion, likely move the paper from a reject to a possible accept.

However, in this case, whilst it would be easy for me to say 'well, youve shown that the optimal level of external pressure varies with environmental parameters, but perhaps it could be interesting to dig into this in more depth?', I'm not sure that will fix a more fundamental issue, which is I'm not clear about the motivation of the paper. I'm not quite sure how to phrase this, and perhaps I should just stop replying (which I probalby will do soonish, maybe after this reply, unsure). Stating that the motivation of the paper seems unclear seems a litte 'he said/she said' to me, so I'd ideally like to formulate that in a more objective/rigorous way, but I'm not quite sure how to do that.

Since there are, as far as I know, many maths-like papers, that go off into a great many esoteric directions, and who's to say that a direction that seems esoteric and niche now won't turn out to be useful at some point in the future?

Indeed, such an accusation seems easy to level against emergent communication as a whole, since it doesn't clearly benefit any currently deployed models, such as chatbots, question and answering etc, which are almost always grounded.

Personally, I like emergent communicaiton as a playground to investigate how language evolved. I dislike the nature of supervised learning on groudned languages where it's not clear if the model is actually being 'clever' in any way, and not just sort of regurgitating by rote learning what it's been taught.

but ok, that's just my own personal preferences. Let's say that it's ok to go off in an esoteric direction. In that case, well then, my reply would be what I allude to earlier: you've shown that the optimal level of external pressure varies with environmental parameters, but perhaps it could be interesting to dig into this in more depth?

Still, I do feel that you might face an up-hill battle in motivating this paper. As the other reviewers allude to, well we have:

-  "I don't understand what the purpose of performing the experiments is, or what conclusions we should draw based on the results. The research question really needs to be made explicit."
- "idid not try to connect back to any natural learning scenarios."

I worry that even if you do go into more depth, and come up with interesting challenges along the way, and interesting solutions to those challenges, that this won't solve the fundamental potential issue that it's not clear how or why other people might use the research?

existing baseline in the generalization ability of language learned
through message exchanges between two neural agents (sender and listener).

The proposed method is to add to the optimization objective of the

objective is reconstruction.  Senders are said to sample from some
message space a certain representation about an object.  The listener
tries to decode the message and reconstruct the object.

the method has an advantage on generalization, the advantage is not
consistent but depends substantially on the agent architecture,
structure of input data, and parameters of the game environment.
content.main_review:
The paper is motivated by an ambitious objective of capturing some
observed advantages of leveraging composition in natural language learning.
It also cites many references in the area for prior art.

On the other hand the paper cannot be read and understood standing
alone as a self-contained piece of work.  The entire discussion is
heavily dependent on assumed
knowledge of the topic, the broader area, and the usual practices of
such simulation experiments.  It does not try to explain what is the
purpose of training, what is supposed to happen in testing, and what
composition and generalization mean in this context.  Therefore the results, even if
it is strong enough to be useful, appeal only to those closely
following the topic. 

The pairing between the object space and the message space is said to

content.main_review:
**Strengths:**

- The paper uses the topological similarity metric [1, 3, 4] commonly used in the emergent communication literature to evaluate compositionality of emergent languages. The key contribution in this paper being the fact that it is used as an additional loss function to explicity tune the pressure for compositionality. To my knowledge, directly optimizing the topological similarity metric has not been studied before which is interesting.
- The paper also includes some evidence that explicitly optimizing this compositionality metric can improve generalization. This insight could be very useful in other NLP settings.
- For the most part, the paper is easy to follow.

**Weaknesses:**

I have included actions that can be taken to strengthen this paper as it stands. However, even with these improvements, it is unlikely that I would recommend the paper to be accepted without drastic changes like including other emergent communication tasks or effects of other types of pressures on emergent languages. 

- **Novelty and Motivation:**
    - Although, to my knowledge, directly optimizing the topological similarity metric has not been studied before, the metric itself is well studied. I am not fully convinced that directly optimizing this metric tells us very much (as is apparent in the experimental section). The paper also bears a lot of similarity to parts of [1].
- **Language Emergence Game and Setup:**
    - The experimental setup is not clear. What are some examples from this dataset? What are some examples of attributes and values? How is it related to other tasks in the literature? Comparisons to the reconstruction task in [2] is made but this does not seem like the same task. It looks similar/identical to the reconstruction task used in [1] but no comparison to that task is made in the paper.
        - **Action:** Improve clarity of the experimental task being used in this paper. Include comparisons to [1].
- **Experiments:**
    - **Figure 1:** The paper claims that carefully tuning the topological similarity metric improves the speed of convergence and generalization. However, this claim is not fully supported due the usage of only 1 learning rate. In particular, 4/6 settings in Figure 1, adding no additional loss performs among the best. In figure 1, a), d), there is evidence that different $C_t$ values performs better but unless additional learning rates and more seeds are used, this claim is not fully supported.

    - **Figure 2:** I don't this that these plot adds much towards the paper. It only seems to work as a sanity check to see if the implementation is accurate. Optimizing a separate loss would naturally improve that loss. It would be more interesting if a different compositionality metric than what was used during training is used instead.
        - **Action:** Use other compositionality metrics like **positional disentanglement [1].**
    - **Table 1, Table 2:** These tables are missing descriptions and does not depict the metrics being measured. The tables are also missing confidence intervals which makes drawing any conclusion from these tables misleading.
        - **Action:** Add descriptions to the tables and include confidence intervals.

We think this is due to recurrent networks processing inputs sequentially along the message, starting from a fixed position. Hence, it is better to have information neatly distributed along the whole message length. 
*  When the available training data is low (smaller data spaces), the latter correlation becomes stronger.
* When agents can train better, the strength of correlation becomes higher. 
* In addition, we observe evidence that further strengths claims of (Chaabouni et al) like:- Positive effect of large input spaces

To the best of our knowledge, (Chaabouni et al) does not employ such external pressure in their study. The advantages offered by our loss are twofold:
* First, it increases the generalization of emergent languages by various amounts depending on the environment parameters (Appendix B)..
* Secondly, when the input space is large, where both our method and the baseline can converge to good generalizing representations, we show that our method can achieve significant improvements in transmission speeds compared to the baseline (Section 4.2.3) .

3. Furthermore we discuss on the behavior of the external pressure with respect to other environment parameters.
* Instances, with recurrent listeners and small amount of training data, gets the most improvement in generalization.
* Higher compositional pressures are favored when vocabulary size is small and messages are longer.

Do they propose such a mechanism was present in the evolution of human language? Or are they finding evidence that rejects this? Are they suggesting it be used in evolving communications in multi-agent environments? To be clear, I cannot see what research question is being asked, and I cannot see what the authors conclude about this question from the evidence they obtain.

The abstract and introduction introduces the general field and makes clear what the experiments involve. As noted above, this fails to articulate what issue the experiments are contributing to.

The relationship to past work is good. There is a sensible quantity of material cited throughout and the material referenced shows how the work fits into the existing material in the area. The bibliography contains a large proportion of papers from arXiv. This is not a peer reviewed source - we have no way of knowing whether claims in these papers meet normal professional criteria. I would guess most of this work actually has been published somewhere - please cite the published version.

The description of the method appears to contain all the necessary details. It is sometimes a little hard to follow. It would be useful to have a non-technical overview in which the basic idea is described without getting bogged down in the details of the networks or using algebra. I didn't follow section 3 very well - I think more detail is needed on Chaabouni et al's measure of compositionality, as it is key to the approach and the paper cannot be fully understood without it.

The experiments seem fine: there is nothing weird in the parameter choices; the factors studied make sense; graphs are clear. There is no comparison to other approaches but this is fine in this work, as it makes no real sense to compare to other methods.

The conclusions do not conclude anything. They are a summary of the experiments and results. They don't tell us what the results mean in terms of any research question.

1. Our main research question is; How to induce compositionality in emergent communications, through a straightforward and simple mechanism? and Whether such externally induced compositonality can increase desirable characteristics like generalization and transmission speed?  

* There is evidence showing that natural languages have a degree of compositionality. Compositional expressions are used by humans to deliver complex ideas using simpler words, hinting it is possible to gain advantages to generalization through compositioinality.

* Existing literature already suggest compositional lanuguages are easier to acquire by new learners.

* Literature contains various approaches for inducing compositionality to boost up emergent communications, including iterative generational transmission and using  supervised pre-training etc, which can be complex.

* If supervised pre-training is used it would require example dialogues, which otherwise entirely not needed for language emergence.

* Iterative generational transmission,inspired by evolutionary linguistics, requires one or more agents to be reinitialized over and over which can be time and resource.

* In this paper, we propose an approach which does not require examples or iterative learning to induce compositionality.

2. We incorporate a novel loss term into the loss function, which is straightforward to implement and does not require additional training cycles, to induce compositionality in controlled manner. We incorporate a well studied metric of compositionality into the training and steer agents to directly optimize the latter metric through their joint loss function. This makes our method straightforward and scalable to various other language emergence setups.

* We show that externally influencing agents via our method, yield improved generalizations and higher speeds of language transmission. 

* We analyse how our method performs with respect to different inputs and message spaces.

It would be useful to have a non-technical overview in which the basic idea is described without getting bogged down in the details of the networks or using algebra. 1. We have included intuitive explanations in to the daft as requested by the reviewer.  And in the below point we will further explain our concepts in a non technical manner.

* Value attribute environment : The dataset used in our experiments appears in many other works including [1,2,3]. In a value attribute environment, a given input consists of a set of finite attributes, where each attribute can take a value. For example, an input with two attributes can be a “Red Square”, which has the attributes of color and shape. For this instance, the attributes color and shape have taken the values “Red” and “Square” respectively. Now if there are values {“Red”, “Blue”} and {“Square'', “Circle”}. This corresponds to a value attribute environment of X(2,2), with two attributes and two values per each. As done by other studies, we do not use direct pixel inputs in the study and employ symbolic inputs [1,2,3], where each value is represented as a one hot encoded vector. Hence, the concatenation of such vectors form an abstract object.

* Compositionality : Agents map environmental entities or concepts with symbols while reaching a consensus for the mapping. If agents follow compositionality, agents would connect individual symbols to atomic concepts in the environment, and combine multiple symbols to form composite messages for expressing complex  concepts, facilitating generalization. For example, Red Square is a compositional expression, containing attributes Color and Shape, constructed by using atomic concepts Red and Square, which corresponds to the values taken by the two attributes. Hence, whenever an agent observes a novel input, it can break down the input into a set of attributes and corresponding values. An expression describing the input can be constructed by suitably concatenating the symbols representing each value of the attributes.

* Generalization :- In this context, generalization means how agents could communicate about unseen combinations of attributes and values. It can be measured by test accuracy similar to other cases in machine learning.

* Reconstruction game : In a reconstruction game, there are two neural agents namely, speaker and listener. The speaker observes a given input and transmits a message consisting of multiple symbols towards the listener. Listener observes the message and reconstructs an approximation of the original input observed by the speaker. Both agents are jointly rewarded according to the degree to which the reconstruction approximates the original input.

[1] Yi Ren, Shangmin Guo, Matthieu Labeau, Shay B Cohen, and Simon Kirby. Compositional languages emerge in a neural iterated learning model. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020

[2] Cinjon Resnick, Abhinav Gupta, Jakob Foerster, Andrew M Dai, and Kyunghyun Cho. Capac-ity, bandwidth, and compositionality in emergent language learning. In Proceedings of the 19th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multi Agent Systems, pp. 1125–1133, 2020

[3] Abhinav Gupta, Cinjon Resnick, Jakob Foerster, Andrew Dai, and Kyunghyun Cho. Compositionality and capacity in emergent languages. InProceedings of the 5th Workshop on Representation Learning for NLP, pp. 34–38, 2020.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer wKT2 (3/3)
content.comment:
>I think more detail is needed on Chaabouni et al's measure of compositionality....

1. Chaabouni et al. proposes three measures for compositionality, but we only use the topological similarity for our experiments. Because it has been used in many other studies and topological similarity can be implemented in a differentiable format using Pearson correlation. 

* Topological similarity: We obtain it as the Pearson correlation between distances of the input pairs and distances of the corresponding message pairs.

* Let's assume three inputs $x1, x2, x3 $ and corresponding messages $m1, m2, m3$.  
* First, all pairs of inputs and messages are obtained:- $[(x1,x2), (m1,m2)], [(x1,x3), (m1,m3)], [(x2,x3), (m2,m3)]$. 
* Next, cosine distance between each pair can be calculated as: $[1-cos(x1,x2), 1-cos(m1,m2)], [1-cos(x1,x3), 1-cos(m1,m3)], [1-cos(x2,x3), 1-cos(m2,m3)].$ 
* This yield the distances between each pair, $[d(x1,x2), d(m1,m2)], [d(x1,x3), d(m1,m3)], [d(x2,x3), d(m2,m3)]$. 
* The topological similarity is defined as the pearson correlation between the two distance sets : $<d(x1,x2),d(x1,x3),d(x2,x3)> $ and $<d(m1,m2),d(m1,m3),d(m2,m3)>$ . 
* The expression $[1-cos(Ah0, Bh0)]$ and [$1-cos(Am, Bm)] $ directly provide the above two vectors.  

Intuitively, Spearman correlation can also be used but its ranking operation is not directly differentiable.

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer WEY2
content.comment:
First, we highly thank the reviewer for their valuable replies. We will explain our stance and address the reviewers' concerns below.

In the current draft, we only measure compositionality for the cases where we do not employ any type of compositionality loss on the discrete link, which we denote as the baseline scenario.  For this case, we study how generalization and compositionality relate, and find that there is indeed a strong but situational correlation.

In the case, where we use compositionality loss, we demonstrate the addition of  compositionality loss, if used in controlled amounts, can improve generalization and transmission speed than the baseline cases. We do not intend to highlight the correlation between test accuracy and topological similarity, for this case, since both are now being optimized simultaneously. 

Our loss is not based on a mechanism that is seen in human language evolution process, but we do not think that adding a loss does violate the existing practices of language emergence research. For example, there are several works which employ different types of metrics, which measure quality of communications in a human perspective, on the emerging communications . 

Studies have used various losses on emerging messages like; entropy regularization, loss on message length, loss on symbol usage, and selecting messages most understandable to the sender itself [1,2,3]. And humans, like how they try to use the shortest message, use compositional expressions not atomic messages. Hence, we think that adding a compositionality loss, which does not require any additional examples, is not against the existing research. As we understand, the main expectation of language emergence is to develop languages in a grounded manner without explicit supervising examples. In our environment, this property is not violated or removed, and agents still develop communications out of necessity. 

We are motivated to induce compositionality for two reasons; First, we observe natural languages are compositional and humans use natural language to express complex concepts, which hints about possible advantages of compositionality. Secondly, there have been studies, using methods motivated by language evolution, that show the generalizing advantage of compositional languages. In this research, we replace the generational transmission mechanisms with a loss which can be directly optimized, which does not need additional training stages. 

1. Katrina Evtimova, Andrew Drozdov, Douwe Kiela, and Kyunghyun Cho. Emergent communication in a multi-modal, multi-step referential game. In 6th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2018.
2. Edward Choi, Angeliki Lazaridou, and Nando De Freitas. Compositional obverter communication learning from raw visual input. In 6th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2018.
3. Angeliki Lazaridou, Karl Moritz Hermann, Karl Tuyls, and Stephen Clark. Emergence of linguistic communication from referential games with symbolic and pixel input. In 6th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2018.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.comment:
This work presents a proposal for increasing the compositionality of emergent languages that uses a measure of topographic similarity as an auxiliary loss function on the communication game. The authors find that in certain cases this loss indeed results in increased generalization but overall the authors do not find a strong relation between high weights for weighting loss and and generalization.
All reviewers agree that the of compositionality is very important and the idea of explicitly optimizing for compositionality (through the topographic similarity metric) is also novel. At the same time a number of concerns are raised by reviewers: 

a) B3Jo and WEY2 raise the point that more evidence is required to establish the robustness of the current findings, e.g., by controlling whether topsim is merely inducing a regularization behaviour and providing more confidence on the current presented results (e.g., Figure 2 currently provides a somewhat perplexed pictured as the additional loss doesn't seem to improve across the board).

b) The relation between compositionality and generalization is not a new one and it is not clear what exactly the current paper is adding on this discussion and, as zB6g and  B3Jo point, this makes it seem rather incremental.

c) the paper is currently somewhat hard to follow with numerous results reported in a somewhat raw format, little to no examples and important details being presented only in Appendix (e.g., the loss function is only given in p12 and the actual format of L_{C} is never provided)

As such, I cannot recommend acceptance at this time but, given the importance of the topic, I sincerely hope the authors will work on incorporating reviewers' feedback for a later resubmission.
